name: Prakash
definition: Prakash is a composite portrait of a Kuruba man in his mid-forties who supervises the ginning floor at a small private cotton mill in Byadgi town, Haveri district. He embodies the experience of industrial workers in the Haveri cotton belt who have navigated two decades of price volatility, mill closures and the squeeze between farmers' distress and mill owners' margins.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Prakash works the morning shift at a ginning mill on the Ranebennur road, arriving at six and leaving by three in the afternoon. He supervises eight workers who feed raw cotton into the gin stands, bale the lint and separate the seed for the oil press. During the October-to-February ginning season he earns around sixteen thousand rupees a month; off-season he takes on repair work, painting jobs and occasional MGNREGA labour to keep some income flowing. The mill has run only four months in the last year because cotton prices crashed to thirty-five hundred rupees per quintal in early 2024, leaving farmers and gin owners both squeezed. Prakash cycles four kilometres each way and carries lunch from home—jowar rotti and shenga chutney most days. He worries that the mill may not open next season if prices stay low and onion farmers switch away from cotton altogether.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Prakash lives in a rented two-room house in Byadgi's Kuruba colony with his wife Leelavati, who works as a domestic helper in three households, and their three children. His eldest daughter Kaveri, aged twenty-two, completed a BA through correspondence and now works as a shop assistant in Haveri town; she sends home two thousand rupees each month. His son Kiran is in second-year pre-university at the government college in Byadgi, studying commerce, and his younger daughter Anusha is in Class 9 at the Kannada-medium high school. Prakash's mother, now seventy, lives with his brother in their village near Hirekerur and receives the widow pension. Leelavati manages the household budget tightly, juggling ration-card rice under Anna Bhagya, Gruha Lakshmi instalments that sometimes arrive late, and loans from a self-help group and a private moneylender. Gender roles are traditional but Prakash insists both daughters study as far as his son does.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Prakash completed Class 7 in his village school before leaving to work on his father's farm and then as a mill hand. He regrets not finishing school and is determined that all three children complete at least pre-university. Kaveri's BA was hard-won—she studied at night after helping at home, and Prakash borrowed from a chit fund to pay the exam and convocation fees. Kiran travels by bus to the government college; the recent free bus pass for students has saved the family about six hundred rupees a month, a relief Prakash mentions often. Anusha attends the town high school, walking twenty minutes each way with classmates. Prakash hopes Kiran will pass the second PU exams and find an office job or join a bank, and that Anusha will finish SSLC and take up nursing or teacher training. He worries about college fees and the cost of competitive-exam coaching in Hubballi if Kiran aims for a government post.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Prakash suffers from chronic cough and occasional breathlessness, the result of inhaling cotton dust for two decades; he has never had a formal lung check but buys cough syrup from the town pharmacy when it worsens. Leelavati has anaemia and took iron tablets during her last pregnancy but stopped after a few months because they made her nauseous. The family goes to the government primary health centre in Byadgi for fevers and minor ailments, and once took Anusha to the taluk hospital in Haveri when she had dengue during the 2023 monsoon. Serious cases mean a referral to Haveri district hospital or even KIMS Hubballi, which costs travel, tests and lost wages. They have an Ayushman Bharat card but have not used the cashless facility yet. Prakash's mother has diabetes and his brother struggles to afford her monthly medicines. Heat during April and May is exhausting, and water supply in the colony is intermittent; the family stores water in drums and boils it during the monsoon to avoid diarrhoea.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Prakash is Kuruba, a community with a strong presence in Haveri district and pastoral and farming roots. He and his family worship at the Hanuman temple near the colony and visit the Kaginele Kanaka Guru Peetha during the annual fair; the peetha's demand for Scheduled Tribe status for Kurubas is a matter of pride and ongoing political talk in the colony. Prakash also attends the Devaragudda Mailara jatra in the district, where thousands gather and the karnika delivers prophecies. His wife is part of a neighbourhood self-help group that meets fortnightly and lends to members at modest interest; Leelavati values the group's savings discipline and mutual support more than any government scheme. Caste is not openly discussed every day, but Prakash is conscious of Lingayat mill owners and Jain traders holding economic power in Byadgi, while Kurubas, Dalits and Muslims form the labour force. Social ties are strongest within the colony, around the temple and at life-cycle events—weddings, naming ceremonies and funerals—where the community pools resources and labour.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He values the five guarantees in principle—Shakti helped his daughter travel to Haveri for her shop job, and Gruha Lakshmi instalments, though delayed, ease the monthly budget when they arrive. The thirty-second instalment came in August 2026, two months behind schedule, and Leelavati had to borrow to cover the gap. Prakash has worked a few days under MGNREGA but finds the seventy days insufficient and wage payment slow. He has never dealt directly with the taluk office beyond getting a caste certificate and ration card; for most government interactions he relies on a local agent who charges fifty or a hundred rupees. He hears talk at the mill and tea stalls about the demand for a Kittur Karnataka development board to match Kalyana Karnataka's Article 371(J) funds, and he agrees that Haveri and the region are overlooked compared with Bengaluru. The winter session at Belagavi's Suvarna Soudha feels ceremonial to him, not a source of real local power or investment.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Prakash worries most about income stability—whether the mill will operate next season, whether Kiran will find work after PU, and whether Anusha will marry before finishing her studies, as happened to two girls in their colony last year. He is proud that his children speak Kannada confidently, that Haveri's SSLC results rank near the top in the state, and that he has kept the family intact without migrating for sugarcane cutting, unlike some neighbours. He blames cotton and onion price crashes on middlemen, government neglect and global markets he does not fully understand, but he also faults local politicians for making promises at election time and vanishing afterward. He respects the Kaginele peetha's leaders and feels that the mutt-run hostels and free meals do more for Kuruba children than government schools alone. Prakash is frustrated that outsiders lump Haveri with either the Hubballi-Dharwad belt or the Kalyana Karnataka region, when it has its own cotton, chilli and onion economy and its own struggles. He demands stable crop prices, permanent jobs at the mill, better water supply in the colony and proper TB and lung-disease screening for mill workers. He wants his children to escape the mill floor and the cycle of off-season debt, and he pins that hope on education, government jobs and the occasional good harvest.
